Title: Philadelphia 2020-2025 Collision Analysis
Abstract: This project investigates which factors are most associated with evident injuries in Philadelphia collisions and how key crash characteristics vary across the city’s 18 planning districts. Using 2020–2025 collision data, we applied logistic Lasso, relaxed logistic regression, and backward elimination to develop a final severity model. Person count, motorcycle involvement, street type, collision type, heavy trucks, pedestrians, and unbelted occupants were important predictors. Separate district regressions found higher bicycle involvement in South, motorcycle and unbelted involvement in North, and heavy-truck involvement in Lower South and Lower Southwest. Geographical features of Upper North, Upper Northeast, and Lower Northeast contribute to a higher rate of severity crashes. These results can help Philadelphia target infrastructure, education, enforcement, and funding toward specific district needs.

Title: Can we Predict Dementia?
Abstract:
For our final presentation we decided to do Dementia. The reason why we picked this topic is because this neurodegenerative condition is becoming more prevalent in society every year. In fact, researchers have predicted approximately 10 million new cases every single year, with around 190 million cases in 2070. 
	The very first component of our EDA is our “variable heatmap correlation”. In this chart, the relationship between variables is established, on a scale of 1 to -1. Through this it becomes apparent that the MMSE exam, education, and nWBV (whole brain volume) have the most direct correlation to dementia. The next section of our EDA is the Dementia vs MMSE score chart. This graph showcased that regardless of there not being a complete “cutoff” between the scores of dementia patients and healthy patients, dementia patients tend to score a 26, while healthy patients score a median of 29. We also used a logistic regression to create our own version of the MMSE test using 16 regressions, with the content originating from our data set (this would be considered one of our models). Next, on our slides there is a chart showcasing the differences between the genders, showing that 58 percent of males have dementia, while only 33 percent of women in our data set tested positive for dementia. Additionally, we have a chart showcasing the MMSE vs. nWBV in patients, which brought the results that MMSE scores separate more than nWBV, but there is still heavy overlap where dementia patients still score high on the MMSE. Furthermore, our next graph demonstrates a correlation between education levels versus dementia. This graph creates overlap between the two box plots, with non-dementia patients having around 16 years of education, and dementia patients having a median of 14 years of education. Lastly for our EDA, we did a chart of Age Vs. nWBV, which displays that the age of dementia patients varies, and that the nWBV. Also from this graph, a trend was noticed that each of these variables impact the probability of getting dementia independently, even after accounting for the overlap in the graph.
	For our created models, we did two logistic regressions (accounting for the model discussed in the previous paragraph), one confusion matrix/neural network, and one random forest. The second logistic regression was made to showcase how each variable impacts the odds of an individual getting dementia. The most significant predictor found was the MMSE test. The confusion matrix was created to identify the number of false positives. The random forest ranks the predictors based on their importance.  
	As for our limitations, we had a lot of data that had to be cleaned, we had a small sample, and we only had a limited number of variables that we could use.

Title: Predicting the Philadelphia 76ers' Regular Season Ranking Using Predictive Models
Abstract: Our goal for this project is to predict 76ers' next year in season ranking, using 30 years of historical data and using models (Linear Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost). The most important variables for a better ranking are offensive rating, defensive rating, and effective field goal percentage, according to our findings and trends.

Title: Pushing Past Averages: Predicting Adulting Illiteracy Risk Across US Counties and Mapping Election Outcomes
Abstract:
We see literacy’s prominence in every aspect of our daily lives, from civic and political communication to interpreting complex texts to employment and education. 
          Though it serves as a foundational backbone for all we do, it is jarring that low literacy is a widespread and geographically erratic problem across the United States of America. Did you know that the percentage of US adults aged 16-74 performing at or below Level 1 in literacy has increased from 19% in 2017 to 28% in 2023?
          Because literacy underpins employment, education, and civic life — and low literacy is widespread but unevenly distributed — we were motivated by this statistic to analyze all 3,141 U.S. counties plus Washington, D.C., using the NCES PIAAC Skills Map's small-area estimates, asking three questions: can socioeconomic and demographic conditions predict literacy and flag high-risk areas; what explains age-specific disparities; and how does literacy relate to voting. LASSO-selected multiple regression predicted county literacy extremely well (R² = 0.84 for both average score and the share at or below Level 1), showing that county literacy tracks measurable local conditions. Our random-forest model then targeted a surprising disparity we found: adults 25–34 outscore those 16–24, the reverse of the expected pattern. Poverty, limited educational attainment, labor-force nonparticipation, and foreign-born share (the only inverse relationship) were the most influential predictors, but at R² = 0.26 the gap remains largely unexplained — a clear direction for future research. Finally, literacy alone predicted 2020 Democratic two-party vote share modestly (R² = 0.27, RMSE 14.1). Adding county controls raised this to R² = 0.80 (RMSE 7.3), while removing literacy from the full model cost only 0.004 held-out R² — a statistically significant association with little unique predictive value once county context is considered.
          As a whole, we see that our findings showcase literacy as a promising and potent indicator of educational and economic structures that can provide opportunities to areas lacking in support.

Title: What Makes a County Red or Blue?
Abstract: Many factors and variables govern partisanship. The goal of this project is to find and determine the statistical significance and association strength of those variables on political partisanship in counties. The dataset used was composed of the selective combination of various other data sources from the Census, USDA, U.S. Religious Census, and a Github repository of all presidential elections since 2016. All counties in Connecticut and with erroneous religious data were excluded due to data reporting issues. Linear regression, neural networks, single decision trees, and random forest were the methodologies applied. Findings indicated the strongest association, that was universal across all used models, was between the percent of bachelor’s degree and Above attainment in a county and Democratic vote share. Other significant correlations include racial variables such as the percent of non-Hispanic Whites and African Americans within the county. Overall, neural networks performed the best at prediction, with a MAE (Mean Absolute Error) of 4.34 or 0.28 SDs of the democratic percentage by county distribution. Neural networks, furthermore, had no outliers outside a 2 SD threshold. Limitations include the relatively minor, but still unideal exclusion of previously mentioned counties (38 in total) due to data issues. Religious data was collected through surveys of denominations, introducing the possibility of imprecise data. Finally, the future predictive power of this project on other future elections will likely lose strength as political coalitions generally shift through the years.

Title: Factors Associated With Severe Traffic Accidents.
Abstract: Our goal was to analyze the factors most associated with the severity of traffic accidents, which was defined as how much impact on the flow of traffic an incident has. To analyze the data, we conducted an EDA and developed three different models: an ordinal logistic regression model, a random forest model, and a neural network. We found that road infrastructure has the strongest association with traffic accident severity, and weather conditions have a more modest, but still notable association.

Title: What Makes a County Bounce Back?
Abstract: Economic recessions have widespread impacts on employment, income, and quality of life, making it important to understand what factors help communities recover more quickly. This study examines county-level recovery following two major U.S. economic downturns: the 2008 Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. By comparing these two recent economic crises, we aimed to identify characteristics associated with stronger economic recovery and provide insights that could help policymakers lessen the effects of future recessions before they occur. We created models using multiple approaches, including separate and combined multiple linear regression models, LASSO regression, and random forest models. Among these, the combined multiple linear regression model produced the strongest performance. The analysis found that higher levels of migration, education, and income were associated with greater recovery, while greater rurality, industry dependence, and larger Black and Hispanic populations were associated with slower recovery. Geographic location also played a role, with counties in the Northeast and South generally experiencing stronger recovery.These findings suggest several policy directions that may improve resilience during future economic downturns, including investing in rural communities, expanding educational opportunities, promoting economic diversification, supporting lower-wealth counties, encouraging migration, and addressing persistent racial inequalities. However, the study has several limitations. The two crises differ in their causes—with one being a medical epidemic while the other being purely economy based—, the models identify associations rather than causation, available data limited the number of predictors included, and some variables contained missing values. Future research could incorporate additional socioeconomic and policy variables, utilize more advanced machine learning methods, compare recovery patterns across other non-U.S.A countries, and develop models capable of predicting community vulnerability before future economic crises occur. Together, these efforts can help governments design policies that strengthen economic resilience and improve quality of life across diverse populations.

Names: Gian-Carlo, Mayon, Jaina, Megan, and Jeffrey
Title: Once Upon a Time: Does Race Decide?
Abstract: Even if online and speed dating have grown in popularity as ways to begin a relationship, it is still challenging to measure the impact of race on who is chosen. We examined the extent to which racial preferences impact an individual's categorical decision to pursue a mate using the speed-dating dataset from the Columbia Business School (6,880 complete-case judgments from 545 participants, 2002–2004). Exploratory data analysis was combined with three classifiers—logistic regression, random forest, and a single-hidden-layer neural network—that were trained on twelve predictors and contrasted with a 0.500 no-skill baseline. The outcome is expected: random forest achieved 0.842 ROC-AUC and 76.1% accuracy. It is not predictable because of racial preference. The combined out-of-sample AUC for own race, partner race, and same-race status was only 0.561; however, the AUC increased by 0.0037 when these factors were included to the six attribute ratings. Even though the raw disparities were significant—an Asian partner earned a yes on 35.4% of dates compared to 46.3% for a European partner (OR 0.63, 95% CI [0.56, 0.72]). However, when the ratings were taken into consideration, the gap was decreased to OR 0.94 (p = 0.44), which accounted for 87% of the difference. The majority group held this preference the strongest, and only same-race preference withstood adjustment (OR 1.19, p = 0.019). The choice was made based on the ratings, which were influenced by race.

Title: Classifying Cancer Using Gene Expression
Abstract:
Our group’s study focuses on finding the minimum number of genes that need to be tested for there to be an accurate enough prediction of a patient’s cancer type. Because more genes means more money and time, by cutting the number of genes we can make testing more affordable and fast.
Our first method uses a data split to narrow the amount of relevant genes from over 58,000 to less than 10. We also created a PCA plot to see whether our data naturally clusters, which it does. Then, we created a few box plots relating genes to cancer type, which tell us that  certain genes correlate with certain types. After this, we ran a LASSO model to shrink the amount of relevant genes from over 58,000 to 7. We did multinomial logistic regression to find that 9 genes is the ideal number to test. We created a neural network and a Random Forest, and we found that there was little improvement compared to using the simpler multinomial logistic regression. 
Ultimately, we concluded that only 9 genes need to be tested rather than 92 to get a high enough accuracy (~91% compared to ~95%). By testing a significantly less amount of genes, the cost of testing can be reduced as well as the time it takes to hear back the results.

Title: An Analysis of Consumer Behavior
Abstract: Customer satisfaction and retention are two important indicators of success in e-commerce. This project investigates two related research questions: (1) Which factors influence the review scores that customers give after a purchase? (2) Which customer, transaction, and delivery characteristics are associated with repeat customers, and how accurately can repeat customers be predicted using information available from their first purchase? Our study uses the Brazilian Olist e-commerce dataset. Exploratory data analysis is first conducted to examine the distribution of review scores and its relationship with several predictors, such as freight cost and delivery time. Our goal is to identify factors associated with review scores, while the models are used to evaluate how well these factors explain and predict categories. We employed logistic regression and neural network for ordinal classification of review scores. We also applied logistic regression, LASSO regression, and random forest to classify whether an order would receive a 5-star review. To predict repeat customers, logistic regression and random forest were trained and evaluated using a train-test split, with predictive performance measured primarily by the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). Our analysis identifies several factors associated with customer satisfaction and repeat purchasing behavior. While meaningful relationships are observed through exploratory and regression analyses, predictive performance for repeat customer classification remains modest, with the best-performing model achieving an AUC of approximately 0.63. These findings suggest that although transaction information contains predictive signals which help in identifying future repeat customers, customer retention depends on additional behavioral and contextual factors, which in addition to first-purchase signals would strengthen the predictor.

Title: After the Crash: What Truly Determines How Long a Crash Disrupts Traffic Flow?
Abstract: Traffic accidents with the same reported severity can disrupt roads for dramatically different lengths of time, raising a critical question: what determines how long a crash impacts traffic? This study investigates the factors that drive crash duration using U.S. accident data containing weather, time, location, roadway features, severity, crash distance, and traffic consequences. We use multiple linear and logistic regression separated by severity levels to identify factors associated with duration while comparing crashes with similar traffic impact, Random Forest to capture nonlinear relationships and interactions among predictors, and a LASSO-assisted neural network to classify crash duration. Our results identify crash distance as the strongest predictor, while weather, time, location, and roadway features vary in impact across severity levels. These findings demonstrate that severity and duration capture different dimensions of a crash and suggest that predictable conditions such as weather and timing can help anticipate prolonged disruptions. Better understanding these duration drivers can support earlier preparation, more efficient traffic management, and more informed driver alerts, while future research can investigate additional operational factors needed to improve crash duration prediction.

Title: A Roof over Every Head: Can We Build Our Way Out
Abstract: Every night, approximately 750000 people are forced to sleep on the streets, at the same time, millions of acres of public land remain undeveloped. This raises the question, could strategic use of land and lower cost housing feasibly reduce homelessness? Using data from national censuses, government reports, and several charities, our aim was to predict the cost of putting a roof over every homeless person in the United States. Through tree based modelling, Exploratory Data Analysis, Regression Techniques, and LASSO, we were able to develop a model that does just that.

Title: Identifying Natural Environmental Factors That Predict Harmful Algal Bloom Development in Western Lake Erie
Abstract: Harmful algae blooms are becoming an increasingly concerning problem in aquatic environments around the world due to their effects on water quality and wildlife. We are interested in determining what natural environmental factors help identify when harmful algal bloom conditions are developing, specifically in western Lake Erie, and whether they could be used to predict future blooms as well. In order to conduct our research, we utilized a number of descriptive statistics and classification models such as neural networks, random forests, and logistic regression with LASSO and ANOVA. Our final model shows that water temperature, baseline particulate and dissolved microcystin concentrations, extracted chlorophyll-a, station depth, and sampling interval are the most critical predictors for forecasting upcoming high-toxin events. By excluding seasonal proxies like month, the LASSO-regularized logistic regression effectively eliminated severe multicollinearity and avoided overfitting, yielding strong out-of-time test performance with an accuracy of 83.98% (77.47% training), a specificity of 92.73%, and an F1 score of 0.6282. These findings confirm that key physical and biochemical parameters, particularly water temperature and dissolved microcystin, serve as robust, interpretable early warning indicators, providing quantitative decision-support for proactive water quality governance in Lake Erie. Thus, we would conduct this research again.
